newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Canada seen vulnerable due to dependence on U.S.
newsitem.headline: Canada seen vulnerable due to dependence on U.S.

text.p: Trading partners expressed concern on Tuesday about Canada's vulnerability because of its heavy dependence on the U.S. economy, senior trade officials said.

Some member states of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) also raised the issue of possible trade injury to non-parties to the North America Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA). Some challenged Canada's high tariffs on textiles and barriers in agriculture.
The debate stemmed from a regular WTO report on Canada's trade policies which said Ottawa's gradual economic and trade liberalisation had boosted the export-driven economy since 1994.

But the report by WTO economists cited persistent concerns about Canada's heavy reliance on trade with the United States. The United States last year bought four-fifths of Canada's goods exports and accounted for two-thirds of its imports.
John Gero, director-general of trade policy at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Trade, represented Canada at the two-day, closed-door talks which ended on Tuesday.
"The importance of the bilateral Canada/USA trade relationship is clear. For each of us the other is our best customer," he told delegates in a speech obtained by Reuters.
Referring to the risk of dependence on one market, he added: "For Canada the risk is simply a reality when we share the continent with the world's economic powerhouse."

Anne Anderson, Ireland's ambassador who chairs the WTO Trade Policy Review Body, told a final news briefing: "Members noted Canada's improved economic performance of the past two years, with growth in exports an important contributing factor.

"However, members came back to the dependence of Canada's economy on the U.S. economy," she said. "While acknowledging that this reflected Canadian firms' ability to operate in a highly competitive market, several members stressed the cyclical vulnerability inherent in such dependence on one destination."
Gero said Canada had been effective in maintaining its share of the U.S. market despite significantly increased competition.

Canadian products and services have had greater success in markets further abroad, he added. Canada's exports to countries other than the U.S. have almost doubled over the last 10 years, growing from $27 billion in 1985 to $52 billion in 1995.
The 137-page study concluded that Canada's overall trade policies remained "firmly anchored in the WTO".

"Concerns persist, however, about the potential vulnerability of the Canadian economy deriving from such high reliance on one large trading partner, on a handful of traditional industries and on relatively few large-scale plants," it said.

"Both 'traditional' industries such as minerals, lumber and automobiles, and 'advanced' sectors have benefited from strong demand in the United States, currency depreciation vis-a-vis the U.S. dollar and liberalisation under NAFTA and the WTO.
Brazil, as well as some other Latin American countries and the Czech Republic were among those expressing concern about possible trade diversion stemming from NAFTA, officials said.
Australia and New Zealand expressed concern about high import barriers to Canada's supply-management regimes for dairy, poultry and egg products, they added.
